steps.label: Binary Search
steps.content:
Algorithm Design and Text Programming

Binary Search

Year 9, 2.4

  • Today: two ways to find a value in a list, and why one is often much faster.
  • You already know: arrays, indexes and loops.
  • Activities: Search Lab: find the middle, then race two searches.
Think → Pair → ShareA dictionary has 1000 pages. Why do you not start at page 1 to find a word?Show the answer

The words are in A to Z order. You can open it near the right place and skip most of the pages.

steps.label: Linear Search
steps.content:
Linear Search

Think → Pair → SharePredict: the target is 40. A linear search starts at index 1. How many items does it check?Show the worked answer

It checks 23, 8, 41, 15, 36, then 40: 6 items. It stops at 40.

Nums

Index12345678
Value238411536401229
  • The value we look for is the target.
  • A linear search checks each item in turn, from index 1.
  • It stops when it finds the target, or when no items are left.
  • Each check is one comparison: is this item the target?

steps.content:
Compare: In Order or Not?

Think → Pair → ShareThe target is 41. Check only the middle item, index 4, in each list. Where could 41 be in A? Where could it be in B? Why?Show the worked answer

A: index 4 holds 26. 41 is bigger, and A is in order, so 41 can only be to the right. Indexes 1 to 4 are not needed.

B: index 4 holds 19. B is not in order, so 41 could be anywhere. Nothing can be skipped.

  • Ordered data is in order: smallest to largest, or A to Z.
  • In ordered data, one check tells you which side the target is on.

steps.label: Binary Search: Check the Middle
steps.content:
Binary Search: Check the Middle

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does binary search throw away the middle item as well as half of the list?Show the answer
The middle item has been checked. It is not the target, so it is not needed again.
  1. Check the middle item.
  2. Is it the target? Stop: found.
  3. Target smaller? Keep the left part.
  4. Target bigger? Keep the right part.
  5. Repeat with the part that is left. Nothing left? The target is not in the list.
  • A binary search finds a target in ordered data.
  • Each comparison throws away about half of the items that are left.

Value5121926344157

Low, High and Middle

Think → Pair → SharePredict: 8 items, so Low = 1 and High = 8. Which index is the middle? Why is there a problem?Show the worked answer

(1 + 8) / 2 = 4.5. There is no index 4.5. Round down: index 4.

Index12345678
Value614212933485267
LowHigh
  • Low is the first index still left. High is the last index still left.
  • Middle = (Low + High) / 2. Not a whole number? Round down.
  • Keep the left part: High = Middle - 1. Keep the right part: Low = Middle + 1.

items.prompt: Which list can a binary search be used on?
items.explain: Binary search needs the data in order. Only 5, 9, 14, 20, 31 goes from smallest to largest.

items.prompt: A list of 500 names is NOT in order. Which search should be used?
items.explain: Linear search checks every item in turn, so order does not matter. Binary search would throw away the wrong half.

steps.label: Exam-Style Question: Describe a Binary Search
steps.content:
Exam-Style Question: Describe a Binary Search

Think → Pair → ShareThis part has 3 marks. How do you plan the answer?Show the answer

Write three different steps, in the order the algorithm does them. One clear step earns one mark.

Answer in full sentences. This part has 3 marks: give three different steps.

items.prompt: Describe how a binary search finds a value in a list. [3]
scheme: The list must be in order / sorted
Compare the middle item with the target
If the middle item is the target, stop / it is found
If the target is smaller, keep the left half / discard the right half
If the target is bigger, keep the right half / discard the left half
Repeat with the half that is left, until it is found or nothing is left (not in the list)
items.guidance: One mark for each point, up to 3. Points 4 and 5 may be made together as one point about discarding the half the target cannot be in, for one mark. Do not accept "it checks every item" or "it splits the list" with no comparison with the middle item.
items.modelAnswer: The list must be in order. Compare the middle item with the target. If it is not the target, throw away the half it cannot be in, and repeat with the half that is left.

steps.label: Exam-Style Question: Compare the Searches (1 of 2)
steps.content:
Exam-Style Question: Compare the Searches (1 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does "it is faster" on its own not earn the mark?Show the answer

The mark is for the reason. Say what the search does that makes the difference.

Give a reason, not just one word.

items.prompt: Give one reason why a binary search is usually faster than a linear search. [1]
scheme: Each comparison discards / halves the items that are left (linear search removes only one item)
It needs fewer comparisons on a long list
items.guidance: One mark for either point. Do not accept "it is quicker" or "it is faster" with no reason.
items.modelAnswer: Each comparison throws away half of the items that are left.

steps.label: Exam-Style Question: Compare the Searches (2 of 2)
steps.content:
Exam-Style Question: Compare the Searches (2 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is "it is easier" not enough for the mark?Show the answer

It gives no reason. Say what is true about the data or the list that makes the other search a better choice.

Give a reason, not just one word.

items.prompt: Give one reason why a linear search might be used instead. [1]
scheme: The data is not in order / is unsorted (binary search needs ordered data)
The list is very short / the target is near the start
items.guidance: One mark for either point. Do not accept "it is easier" with no reason.
items.modelAnswer: The data is not in order, and a binary search only works on ordered data.
